title: Endodontics: root canal treatment
blurb: Pulpotomy, pulpectomy and the stages of root canal treatment, with rubber dam, irrigation safety and the endo set-up.
question: A lower molar has an infected pulp. Rubber dam is on and the dentist has opened the pulp chamber. They ask for the apex locator, then for sodium hypochlorite, and later the paper points keep coming out wet. What stage is each step, and what do the wet points tell you?

teach.h: Saving a tooth from the inside
teach.body: When decay or trauma lets bacteria reach the pulp, it becomes inflamed (pulpitis) and may die and form an abscess at the root tip. Instead of extracting the tooth, endodontic treatment removes the damaged pulp, cleans and disinfects the canals, and seals them. As the nurse you set up and run a demanding procedure: rubber dam, irrigants, tiny files, measurements and radiographs, all under strict asepsis.

teach.h: Why root canal treatment is needed
teach.caption: Infection has spread through the pulp and out of the apical foramen, forming an abscess in the bone at the root tip.

rows.label: Often used for
values: First stage of RCT; emergency relief

teach.caption: A pulp cap covers a tiny exposure of a healthy pulp without removing any pulp at all.

steps.label: Isolate
steps.sub: Local anaesthetic, then rubber dam and clamp

steps.label: Access
steps.sub: Open the pulp chamber, find the canals

steps.label: Dry
steps.sub: Paper points until they come out dry

steps.label: Obturate
steps.sub: Gutta-percha and sealer, then seal the crown

teach.caption: If treatment takes more than one visit, the canals are dressed with a medicament (often non-setting calcium hydroxide) and sealed with a temporary filling. A radiograph checks the final root filling.

1: tray of syringes and small consumables, as irrigants are prepared. 2: operating microscope for magnification. 3: an electronic unit with leads, like an apex locator. 4: rubber dam sheet and clamp. 5: files in a file stand. 6: files in the canals of an isolated tooth during instrumentation.

teach.body: Root canal treatment is always done under rubber dam. It keeps saliva and bacteria out of the canals, stops the patient inhaling or swallowing tiny files, and keeps sodium hypochlorite out of the mouth. If the dam tears or leaks, tell the dentist straight away so they can re-isolate. Files and reamers are single-use, and a dropped file is replaced with a sterile one of the same size and type.

Sodium hypochlorite dissolves pulp tissue and kills bacteria, so it is used repeatedly throughout shaping to flush out debris and disinfect. Forced beyond the root tip, it causes severe pain and swelling. So: draw it into a clearly labelled syringe with a side-vented needle; discard any unlabelled syringe; give the patient safety glasses and protect their clothes. EDTA may also be used to remove the smear layer.

teach.caption: The number is the tip diameter in hundredths of a millimetre. Pass files in size order, with rubber stops set to the working length.

It means / do this
rows: Canal not dry enough to obturate yet
Canal fluid or file position affecting it

teach.text: PulpOTOMY takes the top off (crown pulp only; root pulp stays alive). PulpECTOMY removes all of it. And the order of RCT after access is: working length, clean and shape with irrigation, dry, obturate.

items: Pulpotomy: crown pulp only. Pulpectomy: all pulp, the start of RCT.
RCT: isolate, access, working length, clean and shape with irrigation, dry, obturate, seal.
Rubber dam is mandatory: asepsis, airway protection, keeps hypochlorite out of the mouth.
Hypochlorite: labelled syringe, side-vented needle, patient eye protection; irrigate throughout.
Apex locator = working length; microscope = magnification; wet paper points = not dry yet.

summary: You can now tell pulpotomy from pulpectomy, put the stages of root canal treatment in order, identify the apex locator, microscope, files and rubber dam in an endo set-up, handle sodium hypochlorite safely, and act on warning signs such as wet paper points, a torn dam or a dropped file.

A.q: Rubber dam is on and the pulp chamber of a lower molar has been opened. Which sequence comes next?
options: Obturate, dry, measure length, shape
Shape, obturate, measure length, dry
Measure length, shape and irrigate, dry, obturate
Dry, measure length, obturate, shape and irrigate
A.why: After access, the canal length is measured, the canals are cleaned and shaped with irrigation, dried with paper points, then filled (obturated).

whyNot.0: Obturation is the final step, not the first.
whyNot.1: Canals can't be obturated before they are measured and dried.
whyNot.3: Drying comes after shaping, and obturation is last.

A.q: An apex locator is used during root canal treatment on an upper premolar. What does it help the dentist find?
options: The working length of the canal
Whether the pulp is still vital
The shade for the final crown
The patient's bite after treatment
A.why: An apex locator detects the end of the root canal electronically, giving the working length for files and filling.

whyNot.1: Vitality is tested with cold or electric pulp testers.
whyNot.2: Shade is chosen with a shade guide.
whyNot.3: The bite is checked with articulating paper.

A.q: A file is dropped onto a non-sterile surface during canal preparation. What should you do?
options: Wipe it with alcohol and pass it back
Pass the next file size up instead
Rinse it in hypochlorite and reuse it
Swap for a sterile file of that size
A.why: A contaminated file must not enter the canal. Replace it with a sterile one of exactly the same size and type so the sequence isn't disrupted.

whyNot.1: Skipping a size can damage the canal shape.
whyNot.2: Rinsing in irrigant doesn't sterilise a file, and files are single-use.

B.q: Which statement best describes a pulpotomy?
options: Removal of all pulp from crown and roots
Crown pulp removed, root pulp left vital
Covering a small pulp exposure without removal
Filling the root canals with gutta-percha
B.why: A pulpotomy removes only the coronal (crown) pulp; the radicular (root) pulp stays alive.

whyNot.2: That is a direct pulp cap.
whyNot.3: That is obturation, the final stage of root canal treatment.

B.q: After irrigation, paper points placed in the canal keep coming out wet. What does this most likely mean?
options: The canal is ready to obturate
The working length is too short
The canal still needs more drying
The patient needs more anaesthetic
B.why: Paper points absorb fluid. While they come out wet, the canal isn't dry enough to fill, so drying continues.

whyNot.0: Wet points mean the canal is NOT ready.
whyNot.3: Moisture in the canal isn't related to anaesthesia.

B.q: You notice sodium hypochlorite has been drawn into an unlabelled syringe on the tray. What is the best action?
options: Use it, as it's probably hypochlorite
Discard it and draw up a labelled one
Label it from memory and carry on
Ask the patient to confirm its smell
B.why: Unlabelled syringes risk the wrong solution being injected into the canal. Discard it safely and prepare a clearly labelled one.

whyNot.0: 'Probably' isn't safe with a caustic irrigant.
whyNot.2: Labelling from memory can't guarantee the contents.
whyNot.3: The patient should never be asked to identify a drug.

C.q: During root canal treatment, the rubber dam tears near the clamp and saliva starts to leak in. What should you do?
options: Inform the dentist so they can re-isolate
Pack cotton wool over the tear
Increase the irrigant flow
Finish quickly before more saliva leaks in
C.why: Isolation has been lost, letting bacteria into the canal, so the dentist needs to know immediately to re-establish it.

whyNot.1: Cotton wool won't restore a proper seal.
whyNot.2: More irrigant doesn't stop saliva getting in and risks irrigant leaking into the mouth.
whyNot.3: Rushing on with a leaking dam risks reinfecting the canal.

C.q: Why does the dentist irrigate repeatedly during canal shaping instead of only at the end?
options: To keep the files cool and sharp
To flush debris and disinfect
To measure the canal length
To set the sealer more quickly
C.why: Repeated irrigation washes out debris as it's created and keeps disinfecting the canal throughout preparation.

whyNot.0: Irrigation helps lubricate, but its main job is cleaning and disinfection.
whyNot.2: Length is measured with the apex locator and radiographs.

C.q: Which material is most commonly used, with a sealer, to obturate root canals?
options: Zinc phosphate cement
Composite resin
Calcium hydroxide paste
Gutta-percha points
C.why: Gutta-percha points, used with a sealer, fill the cleaned and shaped canals.

whyNot.0: Zinc phosphate is a luting cement for crowns.
whyNot.1: Composite restores the crown, not the canals.
whyNot.2: Non-setting calcium hydroxide is a temporary dressing between visits.

reteach.title: Think of cleaning out a pipe
reteach.question: A blocked, dirty pipe runs through a wall. How would a plumber clean it and seal it so it never blocks again?

blocks.body: First the plumber measures how long the pipe is, so they don't push their brush out of the far end: that's working length. Then they scrub the inside with brushes of increasing size (files), flushing with cleaner as they go (irrigation). Before sealing, the pipe must be bone dry, so they wipe it with absorbent cloths until one comes out dry (paper points). Finally they fill it completely (gutta-percha) and cap the end (the coronal seal). A dust sheet over everything else is the rubber dam.

blocks.h: Clean and shape: the repeating loop

explain.body: Pulp cap: cover a tiny exposure, no pulp removed. Pulpotomy: remove crown pulp, keep root pulp alive (common in baby molars). Pulpectomy: remove all the pulp, which starts root canal treatment.

explain.caption: Decay has reached the pulp. How much pulp is removed decides the procedure.

test.q: A child's lower deciduous molar has a carious exposure. The dentist removes only the pulp in the crown. What is this?
options: Pulpectomy
Direct pulp cap
Pulpotomy
Apicectomy
test.why: Removing just the coronal pulp and leaving the root pulp vital is a pulpotomy.

whyNot.0: A pulpectomy removes all the pulp.
whyNot.1: A pulp cap removes no pulp.
whyNot.3: An apicectomy is surgical removal of the root tip.

explain.body: Rubber dam and clamp, files in a stand with rubber stops, apex locator for working length, irrigant syringes, paper points, gutta-percha, sealer, and often an operating microscope for magnification of the canal anatomy.

test.q: Why is an operating microscope often used in endodontics?
options: To measure the canal's working length
To magnify and light the canal anatomy
To sterilise files between canals
To light-cure the root canal sealer
test.why: The microscope magnifies and illuminates the pulp chamber, helping the dentist find and treat every canal.

whyNot.0: Working length comes from the apex locator and radiographs.
whyNot.2: Files are single-use and arrive sterile.
whyNot.3: Sealers set chemically; a microscope doesn't cure anything.

explain.body: Clearly labelled syringe, side-vented needle that isn't jammed in the canal, patient safety glasses, protect clothing, rubber dam in place. Discard anything unlabelled.

test.q: The dentist asks for the irrigant with a side-vented needle. Why does it matter if the wrong needle is passed?
options: Irrigant may be pushed past the apex
The irrigant will lose its strength
The file will not fit the canal
The apex locator will stop working
test.why: A side-vented needle releases irrigant sideways, reducing the risk of forcing hypochlorite beyond the root tip.

whyNot.1: Needle type doesn't change the irrigant's strength.
whyNot.2: Needles and files are separate items.
whyNot.3: The apex locator isn't affected by the irrigation needle.

explain.body: ISO files are colour-coded by tip size: 15 white, 20 yellow, 25 red, 30 blue, 35 green, 40 black, then the colours repeat. The small 06, 08 and 10 are pink, grey and purple.

test.q: The dentist asks for the next file after a yellow size 20. Which colour do you pass?
options: White
Blue
Green
Red
test.why: After yellow (20) comes red (25) in the ISO sequence.

whyNot.0: White is 15, the size before yellow.
